analysis.one_liner: Lets the Attorney General set safety standards for guns and ammunition and order recalls of dangerous products.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have treated guns, ammunition, and even BB guns like other consumer products: the Attorney General could write safety rules for how firearms are designed and made, order recalls or refunds of defective ones, and fine manufacturers who shipped products that did not meet the rules. It would also require the government to collect and publish data on gun injuries and deaths. The bill died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been people who own or are around guns, who would gain safer product design, warning labels, and the ability to get defective or unreasonably dangerous firearms recalled, repaired, or refunded. Families of gun-injury victims would have gained a new way to sue violators in court, and the public would have gained access to government data on firearm injuries and deaths.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun owners, their families, shooting victims

how_it_helps.text: The Attorney General would be required to write regulations governing the design, manufacture, and performance of firearms and ammunition to reduce or prevent unreasonable risk of injury [S2][S3].

Any person could petition the Attorney General to require the recall, repair, or replacement of, or refunds for, a dangerous firearm product, and the agency would have to answer within 120 days [S2][S3].
The bill would create a private right to sue for damages against anyone violating the act or its regulations, with attorney's fees available to prevailing plaintiffs [S3].

The Attorney General, working with Health and Human Services, would have to collect and publicly release data on the circumstances of firearm deaths and injuries, plus production and sales figures for each licensed manufacturer [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers (including pawnbrokers) would bear the costs: testing and certifying products before sale, labeling requirements, keeping records open to inspection, complying with safety regulations, paying civil fines of up to $10,000-$20,000 per violation, and footing the bill for recalls, repairs, or refunds. Some of those costs could be passed to buyers as higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The regulatory authority is broad and discretionary: the Attorney General could bar the manufacture, sale, or transfer of any product deemed to pose an 'unreasonable risk,' which critics argued could amount to banning particular guns or models through regulation rather than legislation [S3].
Compliance, testing, labeling, and recall requirements would raise costs for manufacturers and dealers, and those costs could be passed on to buyers through higher prices [S3].

The private enforcement provision would let 'any interested person' sue to restrain violations, which gun-rights opponents warned could be used as a litigation tool against the industry beyond its consumer-protection purpose [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits (safer product design, recalls of defective guns, injury data) are real and mirror what consumers already get for toys, cars, and household products, which guns were exempt from. The costs fall on a concentrated industry and, partly, on buyers through prices. The strongest fair objection is that the Attorney General's power to ban 'unreasonably risky' products gives one executive official sweeping discretion over a constitutionally sensitive product, which opponents could reasonably see as backdoor gun control. On balance the bill was a straightforward consumer-safety measure, but its broad language made that easy to dispute.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day it was introduced, sat there without a hearing or markup, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Corzine, joined by Sen. Frank Lautenberg, introduced the Firearms Safety and Consumer Protection Act of 2003 in the Senate on June 10, 2003 [S1][S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction; that was the last action of any kind recorded [S5].
No hearing, committee vote, floor vote, or further action ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers, importers, and dealers are better off, because they avoided safety standards, testing and certification duties, recall exposure, federal fines, and a private right of action. Anyone opposed to expanded federal authority over firearms design also got the outcome they wanted, without any vote ever being taken on the merits.

for.name: Sen. Jon Corzine
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and gave introductory remarks when it was introduced.

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Joined Corzine in introducing the bill as a cosponsor.

for.name: 1 additional Senate Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total cosponsors to two, both Democrats.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never took it up; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: National Rifle Association and allied gun-rights groups
against.what_they_did: Long opposed subjecting firearms to consumer-product regulation, treating it as a step toward restricting gun ownership.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, but every sponsor and cosponsor was a Senate Democrat, and no Republican supported the bill on the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to test, certify, and label every product, open records to inspection, and recall or refund products deemed defective or unreasonably risky, with fines and lawsuits for violations. Their interest in killing the bill ran against the public's interest in product safety.

'Firearm product' is defined to include ammunition, parts, and accessories, so safety regulations and certification requirements would cover them too. The public would gain consistent safety standards across the products that cause the injuries.

Dealers and pawnbrokers were expressly included in the definition of firearms dealers and would share recall, labeling, and record-keeping duties. Killing the bill spared them compliance costs while leaving buyers without the safety assurances.

industries.industry: Nonpowder firearm (BB and pellet gun) makers
industries.note: The bill expressly brought nonpowder firearms under the Attorney General's jurisdiction. These products injure many children, so safety standards here run alongside the public's interest.
